tagline: Manage the full contract lifecycle using NCMA's Contract Management Standard and CMBOK.

domains.name: Guiding Principles
domains.description: Cross-cutting principles, skills, standards of conduct, and competencies applied across the entire contract lifecycle.

domains.name: Pre-Award: Develop Solicitation
domains.description: The buyer's pre-award work to plan acquisitions and request offers from the market.

domains.name: Pre-Award: Develop Offer
domains.description: The seller's pre-award work to plan sales and prepare a responsive, competitive offer.

domains.name: Award: Form Contract
domains.description: Award-phase activities where buyer and seller analyze price, negotiate, select a source, and form the contract.

domains.name: Post-Award: Perform and Administer Contract
domains.description: Post-award execution: administering performance, ensuring quality, managing subcontracts, and handling changes.

domains.name: Post-Award: Close Contract
domains.description: Completing and closing out the contract, capturing lessons learned, and continuous learning.

questions.stem: A buyer and a seller each appoint a contract manager to oversee the same agreement. What BEST describes the contract manager's fundamental role across the contract life cycle?

options.text: To advocate solely for their own organization and concede nothing to the other side
To draft the technical specification that the engineers will deliver against
To approve all payments without regard to whether performance has occurred
To manage the relationship and the agreement so that both parties' obligations are met and value is realized

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A contract manager stewards both the business relationship and the agreement itself, ensuring obligations are performed and the intended value is delivered to their organization. Why the others are wrong: **A** pure adversarial advocacy ignores the collaborative, value-focused intent of professional contract management; **B** writing the technical specification is the requiring activity's job, not the contract manager's core role; **C** approving payment without verifying performance violates basic stewardship and controls.

questions.stem: During a competitive procurement, a supplier offers a contract manager box-seat tickets to a sporting event "just as a token of appreciation." The most defensible action under accepted standards of conduct is to:

options.text: Accept the tickets but disclose them later if anyone asks
Decline the gift to avoid any conflict of interest or appearance of impropriety
Accept the tickets because they are below a personal comfort threshold
Accept on behalf of the whole team so it is a group benefit

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Ethical standards require contract managers to avoid both actual conflicts of interest and the appearance of impropriety; declining the gift during an active competition protects the integrity of the process. Why the others are wrong: **A** accepting first and disclosing only if asked still creates an appearance problem and shifts the burden improperly; **C** a personal comfort threshold is not a recognized organizational standard; **D** spreading the gift across the team does not cure the conflict during a live source selection.

questions.stem: Under a firm-fixed-price (FFP) contract, the actual cost of performance turns out to be much higher than the seller estimated. Who bears that cost risk?

options.text: The buyer, because the price can be adjusted upward for actual costs
The seller, because the price is fixed regardless of the seller's actual costs
The risk is shared 50/50 between buyer and seller
A third-party surety, who reimburses the overrun

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** In an FFP arrangement the price is set at award and does not change with the seller's actual costs, so the seller absorbs any overrun and keeps any savings—placing maximum cost risk on the seller. Why the others are wrong: **A** the buyer's price is fixed and is not adjusted for the seller's actual costs; **C** FFP does not split overruns, unlike a fixed-price-incentive share line; **D** a surety guarantees performance/payment bonds, it does not reimburse a seller's cost overruns.

questions.stem: Which contract type generally places the GREATEST cost risk on the buyer?

options.text: Firm-fixed-price (FFP)
Fixed-price with economic price adjustment
Cost-plus-fixed-fee (CPFF)
Fixed-price incentive (firm target)

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Under a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract the buyer reimburses the seller's allowable costs and pays a fixed fee, so cost growth flows to the buyer—making it the highest-risk type for the buyer. Why the others are wrong: **A** FFP fixes the price and puts cost risk on the seller; **B** an economic price adjustment shifts only narrow, defined cost movements (e.g., specified materials/labor indices), not general overruns; **D** a fixed-price incentive caps buyer exposure at the ceiling price and shares overruns by the share ratio.

questions.stem: A time-and-materials (T&M) contract is being considered for a repair effort of uncertain scope. Which statement about T&M is correct?

options.text: It guarantees a fixed total price regardless of hours expended
It reimburses the seller's costs plus a percentage of cost as fee
It transfers all schedule and cost risk to the seller
It pays fixed labor-hour rates plus materials at cost and requires close buyer surveillance because the seller has little incentive to control hours

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** T&M pays fixed hourly labor rates plus materials and is used when scope can't be estimated precisely; because billing rises with hours, the buyer must actively monitor labor to control cost. Why the others are wrong: **A** T&M has no fixed total price—cost varies with hours and materials; **B** percentage-of-cost fee is prohibited as a pricing method and is not how T&M works; **C** T&M leaves significant cost risk with the buyer, not the seller.

questions.stem: Which two behaviors are core expectations of a contract management professional's standards of conduct? (Select two.)

options.text: Protect proprietary and source-selection information from unauthorized disclosure
Act with integrity, honesty, and impartiality in dealings with all parties
Maximize personal benefit from each transaction
Share a competitor's confidential pricing with another bidder to drive prices down

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Safeguarding proprietary and source-selection information and acting with integrity, honesty, and impartiality are foundational duties in any recognized contract-management code of conduct. Why the others are wrong: **C** seeking personal gain from transactions is a conflict of interest, not a professional standard; **D** disclosing one bidder's confidential pricing to another is a serious integrity and procurement-fairness violation.

questions.stem: A contract manager realizes that a clause in a draft agreement would require conduct that violates an applicable law or regulation. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Sign the contract and address the legality issue only if it is ever challenged
Raise the issue and ensure the contract is brought into compliance before agreement, even if it delays award
Leave the clause in but privately agree with the other party not to enforce it
Delegate the decision to the technical team since it is their requirement

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Regulatory compliance is non-negotiable; the contract manager must surface the conflict and have the agreement corrected before commitment, accepting schedule impact rather than agreeing to unlawful terms. Why the others are wrong: **A** knowingly signing an unlawful clause exposes the organization to legal risk and breaches the duty of compliance; **C** a private side understanding not to enforce an illegal clause is itself unethical and unenforceable; **D** legality is a contract-management/legal responsibility, not something to push onto the technical team.

questions.stem: Before issuing any solicitation, a buyer studies the supplier base, available technologies, and typical pricing for a commodity it intends to purchase. This activity is called:

options.text: Source selection
Contract closeout
Quality assurance surveillance
Market research

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Market research is the systematic gathering of information about available products, suppliers, technologies, and pricing to shape requirements and the acquisition strategy before solicitation. Why the others are wrong: **A** source selection happens after offers are received, not before solicitation; **B** closeout is the final life-cycle phase after performance; **C** quality surveillance occurs during contract performance, not pre-solicitation planning.

questions.stem: A buyer needs a standardized commodity where the requirement can be described precisely and award will be based on lowest price among responsive, responsible bidders. Which solicitation method fits BEST?

options.text: Request for Proposals (RFP) with best-value tradeoff
Invitation for Bids (IFB) using sealed bidding
Request for Information (RFI)
Sole-source negotiation

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** An IFB / sealed bidding is appropriate when the requirement is well defined and award goes to the lowest responsive, responsible bidder on price, with no need for discussions. Why the others are wrong: **A** an RFP with best-value tradeoff is for situations where non-price factors and negotiations matter; **C** an RFI only gathers information and does not result in award; **D** sole-source negotiation is used when only one source can meet the need, not for a competitive commodity buy.

questions.stem: A complex services acquisition will weigh technical approach, past performance, and price, and the buyer expects to hold discussions before award. Which document should the buyer issue?

options.text: Invitation for Bids (IFB)
Request for Quotation (RFQ) for a micro-purchase
Request for Proposals (RFP)
Purchase order with no terms

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** An RFP is the right vehicle when award depends on multiple evaluation factors (technical, past performance, price) and the buyer may conduct discussions and tradeoffs before selecting an offer. Why the others are wrong: **A** an IFB allows no discussions and awards strictly on price; **B** an RFQ is for relatively simple, low-dollar buys and quotations are not offers; **D** a bare purchase order lacks the structured evaluation needed for a complex, negotiated services buy.

questions.stem: Evaluation criteria in a solicitation should BEST be:

options.text: Kept secret from offerors so the buyer retains flexibility to decide after offers arrive
Disclosed in the solicitation and used to evaluate offers as stated
Changed after offers are received to favor the preferred vendor
Limited to price only in every acquisition

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Fair, defensible source selection requires that evaluation factors and their relative importance be stated in the solicitation and then applied exactly as written. Why the others are wrong: **A** concealing the criteria undermines fairness and offerors' ability to compete responsively; **C** altering criteria after receipt to favor a vendor is a serious integrity breach; **D** price-only evaluation is appropriate for some buys but is not required for all—best-value tradeoffs are common.

questions.stem: A buyer faces a research effort with significant technical unknowns and cannot define the scope precisely enough to set a fair fixed price. Which pricing arrangement is generally most appropriate?

options.text: Firm-fixed-price, to cap the buyer's cost
A cost-reimbursement type, which suits high uncertainty by reimbursing allowable costs
A fixed-price requirements contract
A purchase order priced at the catalog rate

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** When requirements are uncertain and costs cannot be estimated with confidence, a cost-reimbursement type is appropriate because the seller is reimbursed allowable costs, which would otherwise be unpriceable under a fixed price. Why the others are wrong: **A** forcing FFP onto an ill-defined effort transfers unquantifiable risk and inflates contingency or invites failure; **C** a requirements contract still needs a definable, priced scope; **D** a catalog-priced purchase order assumes a standard, well-defined item, not novel research.

questions.stem: Which two items are typically established during acquisition planning, before the solicitation is released? (Select two.)

options.text: The final negotiated price with the winning offeror
The contractor's past-performance rating after this contract closes
The requirement/statement of need and the acquisition strategy
The contract type and competition approach

questions.explanation: **Correct (C, D):** Acquisition planning defines what is needed and how it will be bought—the requirement and overall strategy, including the contract type and whether/how competition will occur. Why the others are wrong: **A** a negotiated price is set during contract formation, after offers are received; **B** a past-performance rating for this contract is generated during/after performance, not in pre-solicitation planning.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of a Statement of Work (SOW) or Performance Work Statement (PWS) in a solicitation?

options.text: To list the buyer's internal budget reserves
To replace the need for any evaluation criteria
To serve as the seller's invoice
To define the work to be performed or the outcomes required so offerors can propose and the buyer can measure performance

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A SOW/PWS describes the required work or performance outcomes so offerors understand what to propose and the buyer has a basis to evaluate offers and later judge performance. Why the others are wrong: **A** internal budget reserves are not disclosed in the work statement; **B** a SOW defines work but does not eliminate the need for stated evaluation criteria; **C** an invoice is a payment document submitted during performance, unrelated to the SOW's purpose.

questions.stem: A seller is deciding whether to respond to a newly released RFP. Which formal step BEST captures this evaluation of whether pursuing the opportunity makes business sense?

options.text: A bid/no-bid decision
A contract closeout review
A constructive change determination
A final indirect cost rate proposal

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A bid/no-bid decision weighs factors such as fit, probability of win, resources, and risk to decide whether to invest in preparing an offer. Why the others are wrong: **B** closeout review happens after performance ends, not before bidding; **C** a constructive change arises during performance when conduct effectively changes the work; **D** an indirect rate proposal relates to cost accounting/billing, not the decision to pursue an opportunity.

questions.stem: A proposal team notices that one solicitation instruction conflicts with the seller's standard approach. To remain compliant, the team should:

options.text: Ignore the instruction and submit the proposal in the seller's preferred format
Follow the solicitation's instructions exactly, since non-compliance can render the offer unacceptable
Add unrequested information to impress the evaluators and skip the required sections
Submit after the deadline with an explanation

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Offerors must comply with the solicitation's instructions and requirements; a materially non-compliant or non-responsive offer can be rejected regardless of its technical merit. Why the others are wrong: **A** ignoring instructions risks the offer being found unacceptable; **C** padding with unrequested content while omitting required sections increases non-compliance risk; **D** late submissions are routinely excluded and do not cure a compliance problem.

questions.stem: When preparing a cost estimate for a proposal, which estimating method builds the total cost by summing detailed estimates of individual work elements?

options.text: Analogous (top-down) estimating
Parametric estimating using a single rate
Bottom-up estimating
Rough order of magnitude (ROM) only

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Bottom-up estimating aggregates detailed estimates of individual tasks or work packages into a total, generally yielding the most accurate cost picture for a defined scope. Why the others are wrong: **A** analogous estimating uses a similar past effort for a quick top-down figure, with less detail; **B** parametric estimating scales cost from a statistical rate or driver, not a roll-up of work elements; **D** a ROM is a broad early-stage approximation, not a detailed roll-up.

questions.stem: A seller wants to win on price but must still cover its costs and earn a return. In cost-based pricing, the seller's proposed price is generally composed of:

options.text: Direct costs, indirect costs (overhead/G&A), and profit/fee
Only the direct labor hours, with no overhead
The buyer's budget, regardless of the seller's costs
A fixed government-set rate that sellers may not alter

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Cost-based pricing builds price from direct costs (labor, materials), allocated indirect costs such as overhead and G&A, and a profit or fee component. Why the others are wrong: **B** omitting overhead/G&A understates true cost and is unrealistic; **C** the buyer's budget is not the seller's cost basis—price must recover the seller's costs; **D** prices are proposed by sellers, not dictated by a fixed government rate.

questions.stem: Which two factors should most influence a seller's bid/no-bid decision? (Select two.)

options.text: Alignment of the opportunity with the seller's capabilities and strategy
Realistic probability of winning relative to the cost of bidding
Whether the proposal manager personally likes the buyer's logo
The seller's preference to bid on everything regardless of fit

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Sound bid/no-bid decisions weigh strategic and capability fit against the realistic win probability and the cost/effort of pursuing the bid. Why the others are wrong: **C** personal aesthetic preferences are irrelevant to a business decision; **D** bidding on everything wastes resources and ignores fit and win probability.

questions.stem: A seller identifies a major technical risk that could increase costs during performance. In responsible proposal preparation, the seller should:

options.text: Hide the risk so the price looks lower and more competitive
Assess the risk and reflect a realistic mitigation and cost/contingency in the proposal
Assume the buyer will absorb any overrun under any contract type
Remove the affected work from the proposal without telling the buyer

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Risk assessment in proposal preparation means identifying significant risks and reflecting credible mitigation plans and appropriate cost/contingency, producing a realistic, executable offer. Why the others are wrong: **A** concealing risk to lower price leads to under-pricing, performance failure, and potential losses; **C** under a fixed-price type the seller—not the buyer—bears overruns, so the assumption is wrong and dangerous; **D** silently dropping required scope makes the offer non-compliant and misleads the buyer.

questions.stem: A buyer compares an offeror's proposed price to recent prices paid for the same item and to a published market price, without examining the offeror's individual cost elements. This technique is:

options.text: Cost analysis
Price analysis
Should-cost review
Earned value analysis

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Price analysis evaluates the reasonableness of a total or unit price by comparison to other prices (competition, prior buys, market, catalogs) without dissecting the offeror's cost elements. Why the others are wrong: **A** cost analysis breaks down and evaluates the individual cost elements and profit, which this scenario does not do; **C** a should-cost review is an in-depth cost study of how work should be performed; **D** earned value analysis measures performance against a baseline during execution, not price reasonableness at award.

questions.stem: When is cost analysis (rather than price analysis alone) generally REQUIRED to determine price reasonableness?

options.text: When adequate price competition exists and prices can be compared
When there is no adequate price competition and the buyer must evaluate the offeror's individual cost elements
When buying a commercial item at an established catalog price
Whenever the dollar value is below the micro-purchase threshold

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Without adequate price competition or another market basis, the buyer cannot rely on comparison alone and must analyze the offeror's individual cost elements (cost analysis) to judge reasonableness. Why the others are wrong: **A** adequate competition usually allows price analysis by comparison, not full cost analysis; **C** a catalog/commercial price supports price analysis; **D** micro-purchases use simplified methods and do not trigger detailed cost analysis.

questions.stem: In negotiation preparation, a negotiator identifies the least-favorable deal they will accept before walking away. This concept is BEST described as the:

options.text: Opening position
Bargaining range midpoint
Walk-away point (reservation point)
Aspiration (target) point

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The walk-away or reservation point is the minimally acceptable outcome; beyond it, no agreement is preferable to a bad deal. Why the others are wrong: **A** the opening position is the first offer placed on the table, typically more favorable than the limit; **B** the midpoint of the bargaining range is a likely settlement zone, not the limit; **D** the aspiration/target point is the most favorable realistic goal, the opposite end from the walk-away.

questions.stem: A negotiator wants the most durable agreement and focuses on understanding each party's underlying interests rather than rigid positions. This approach is BEST described as:

options.text: Positional (distributive) bargaining
Interest-based (principled) negotiation
Take-it-or-leave-it ultimatum
Avoidance of negotiation altogether

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Interest-based (principled) negotiation explores the parties' underlying interests to craft mutually beneficial, durable agreements rather than haggling over fixed positions. Why the others are wrong: **A** positional bargaining fixates on stated positions and tends to produce win-lose, less durable outcomes; **C** an ultimatum forecloses problem-solving and damages the relationship; **D** avoiding negotiation leaves issues unresolved and is not an approach to reaching agreement.

questions.stem: For a valid, enforceable contract to be formed, which combination of elements is generally required?

options.text: Offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity, and a lawful purpose
Offer and acceptance only, with no consideration needed
A signed document, regardless of consideration or legality
Mutual goodwill, even without any exchange of value

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A binding contract generally requires a valid offer, acceptance, consideration (a bargained-for exchange of value), parties with capacity, and a lawful purpose. Why the others are wrong: **B** consideration is generally essential—an exchange of value supports enforceability; **C** a signature alone cannot validate a contract that lacks consideration or has an illegal purpose; **D** goodwill without any exchange of value lacks consideration and is unenforceable.

questions.stem: An offeror submits a response that changes a material term of the buyer's offer. Under general contract principles, this response is BEST characterized as:

options.text: A valid acceptance forming a contract on the buyer's original terms
A counteroffer, which rejects the original offer and proposes new terms
An option contract binding the buyer
A unilateral mistake that voids all dealings

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A response that alters a material term is a counteroffer; it rejects the original offer and puts a new offer on the table that the other party may accept or reject. Why the others are wrong: **A** changing a material term is not a mirror-image acceptance, so no contract forms on the original terms; **C** an option requires separate consideration to keep an offer open, which is not described; **D** a counteroffer is a normal negotiating move, not a unilateral mistake that voids dealings.

questions.stem: Which two activities are central to effective source selection? (Select two.)

options.text: Evaluating offers against the criteria stated in the solicitation
Documenting the rationale that supports the selection decision
Disclosing one offeror's proprietary data to its competitors
Selecting the vendor before any evaluation is performed

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Effective source selection applies the stated evaluation criteria consistently to all offers and records a clear rationale that supports and defends the award decision. Why the others are wrong: **C** disclosing proprietary data to competitors breaches confidentiality and procurement integrity; **D** picking the vendor before evaluating offers defeats the purpose and fairness of source selection.

questions.stem: Two parties disagree over a pricing assumption late in negotiations. To preserve the relationship and still reach agreement, the contract managers should FIRST:

options.text: Terminate negotiations and issue a formal claim
Identify the underlying interests and explore options that could satisfy both parties
Each insist on their position until one side gives up
Sign the contract and litigate the assumption afterward

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Managing disagreement to reach agreement starts with understanding each side's interests and jointly generating options, which is most likely to produce a workable deal and protect the relationship. Why the others are wrong: **A** terminating and filing a claim is premature before any problem-solving attempt; **C** entrenched positional standoff often deadlocks and harms the relationship; **D** signing first and litigating later builds a known dispute into the contract instead of resolving it.

questions.stem: A written contract contains an integration (entire-agreement) clause. Under the parol evidence rule, what is the general effect on prior oral promises that contradict the written terms?

options.text: Prior contradictory oral promises are generally not admissible to vary the fully integrated written terms
Prior oral promises always override the written contract
The written contract is automatically void if any oral discussions occurred
Oral promises made after signing are barred, but prior ones always control

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** When a writing is fully integrated, the parol evidence rule generally bars prior or contemporaneous oral statements offered to contradict or vary the written terms. Why the others are wrong: **B** prior oral promises do not override an integrated writing; **C** the existence of prior discussions does not void a written contract; **D** the rule addresses prior/contemporaneous statements, not later modifications, and prior oral promises do not 'always control.'

questions.stem: Once a contract is awarded, what is the contract administrator's PRIMARY ongoing responsibility?

options.text: To re-run the source selection periodically
To rewrite the requirements from scratch each month
To stop all communication with the contractor
To monitor both parties' performance against the contract terms and address issues as they arise

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Contract administration centers on monitoring performance against the terms—deliverables, schedule, quality, and payments—and managing issues, changes, and communications as they occur. Why the others are wrong: **A** source selection is a pre-award activity and is not repeated during administration; **B** requirements are baselined in the contract, not rewritten arbitrarily each month; **C** active, documented communication with the contractor is essential to administration, not something to cease.

questions.stem: A contracting officer's technical representative orally directs the contractor to perform extra work beyond the contract's scope, and the contractor complies. This situation is BEST described as a:

options.text: Constructive change
Bilateral modification properly signed by both parties
Novation of the contract
Termination for convenience

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A constructive change occurs when the buyer's conduct or informal direction effectively requires work outside the contract scope without a formal modification, potentially entitling the contractor to an equitable adjustment. Why the others are wrong: **B** a bilateral modification is a formal change signed by both parties—this direction was informal; **C** a novation substitutes a new party to the contract; **D** a termination for convenience ends work, it does not add work.

questions.stem: A change to the contract is agreed to and signed by both the buyer and the seller. This type of modification is called:

options.text: A unilateral modification
A bilateral modification (supplemental agreement)
An administrative change
A constructive change

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A bilateral modification, or supplemental agreement, is signed by both parties and is used when the change affects rights or obligations, such as price, scope, or schedule. Why the others are wrong: **A** a unilateral modification is signed only by the buyer (e.g., within the scope of a changes clause or for administrative actions); **C** an administrative change corrects non-substantive details and does not affect parties' rights; **D** a constructive change is informal direction, not a signed modification.

questions.stem: Under a fixed-price contract with an inspection/acceptance clause, the buyer's inspector finds delivered goods do not conform to specification. The buyer's MOST appropriate first step is to:

options.text: Accept and pay for the goods to keep the relationship friendly
Reject the nonconforming goods and notify the seller, consistent with the contract's inspection and acceptance terms
Immediately terminate the contract for convenience
Ignore the defect and document it only at closeout

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** When goods fail to conform, the buyer should exercise its inspection/acceptance rights—reject the nonconforming supplies and notify the seller so corrective action (repair, replacement, or other remedy) can follow. Why the others are wrong: **A** accepting and paying for nonconforming goods waives the buyer's quality rights and rewards noncompliance; **C** termination for convenience is a drastic step, not the first response to a curable defect; **D** ignoring a defect until closeout undermines quality assurance and remedies.

questions.stem: A prime contractor enters an agreement with a lower-tier supplier to perform part of the prime's contract work. This lower-tier agreement is a:

options.text: Subcontract
Novation
Teaming agreement only
Letter contract

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A subcontract is an agreement between the prime contractor and a lower-tier party to furnish supplies or services for performance of the prime contract; the prime remains responsible to the buyer. Why the others are wrong: **B** a novation substitutes a new party for the original prime, not a lower-tier performer; **C** a teaming agreement is a pre-award arrangement to pursue an opportunity together, not the performance subcontract itself; **D** a letter contract is a preliminary instrument authorizing work to begin before terms are finalized.

questions.stem: A buyer ends a contract for its own business reasons even though the contractor was performing acceptably, using a clause that allows this. This is a termination for:

options.text: Default (cause)
Convenience
Material breach by the contractor
Mutual mistake

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A termination for convenience lets the buyer end the contract (in whole or part) when it is in the buyer's interest, even absent contractor fault, typically entitling the contractor to costs incurred plus a reasonable profit on work done. Why the others are wrong: **A** a termination for default/cause requires contractor failure to perform; **C** material breach by the contractor describes default, not convenience; **D** mutual mistake is a contract-formation doctrine, not a termination right exercised here.

questions.stem: A contractor fails to deliver and offers no acceptable explanation. The buyer terminates the contract for default. If a court or board later finds the default was improper, the default termination is generally:

options.text: Converted to a termination for convenience
Automatically upheld regardless of the facts
Treated as a novation
Converted into a price increase for the contractor

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under the standard default framework, an improper or unjustified termination for default is typically converted to a termination for convenience, limiting the contractor's recovery to convenience-termination remedies rather than breach damages. Why the others are wrong: **B** a wrongful default is not automatically upheld—the conversion remedy exists precisely for that case; **C** a novation substitutes parties and is unrelated to termination disputes; **D** the outcome is a change in termination basis, not an automatic price increase.

questions.stem: On a cost-reimbursement contract, what is a key reason the buyer must actively monitor the contractor's incurred costs and funding status?

options.text: Because the buyer reimburses allowable costs and must manage funding limits and the limitation-of-cost notice
Because the price is fixed and never changes
Because the contractor bears all cost risk and the buyer has nothing to track
Because cost data is irrelevant to performance management

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** On cost-reimbursement work the buyer pays allowable incurred costs, so it must track spend against funding, watch for the contractor's limitation-of-cost/funds notice, and ensure funds are available. Why the others are wrong: **B** cost-reimbursement is not fixed-price—costs vary and must be tracked; **C** the buyer, not the contractor, carries the cost risk here, so monitoring is essential; **D** cost data is central to managing a cost-type contract, not irrelevant.

questions.stem: A contractor submits an invoice for progress payments. Before approving payment, the contract administrator should FIRST verify that:

options.text: The contractor needs the cash flow this month
The amount matches a competitor's invoice
The invoiced work or milestone has actually been performed in accordance with the contract
The buyer has unspent budget it wants to use up

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Payment should follow verified performance—confirming the invoiced work, deliverable, or milestone was actually completed per the contract before authorizing funds. Why the others are wrong: **A** the contractor's cash-flow need is not a basis for approving payment; **B** a competitor's invoice is irrelevant to this contract's earned payments; **D** spending down a budget is not a valid reason to pay for work not yet earned.

questions.stem: Which two are appropriate quality assurance activities during contract performance? (Select two.)

options.text: Accepting any deliverable without inspection to save time
Inspecting deliverables against the contract's specifications and acceptance criteria
Allowing the contractor to self-certify quality with no buyer oversight on a critical effort
Conducting surveillance using a quality assurance surveillance plan (QASP)

questions.explanation: **Correct (B, D):** Quality assurance during performance includes inspecting deliverables against specs/acceptance criteria and surveilling performance under a QASP, especially on services. Why the others are wrong: **A** accepting deliverables without inspection abandons the buyer's quality controls and remedies; **C** unverified contractor self-certification on a critical effort removes necessary oversight and risk control.

questions.stem: As a contract moves toward closeout, several open invoices and a contractor claim remain unresolved. Before the contract can be financially closed, the parties must FIRST:

options.text: Destroy the contract file to save storage space
Award a follow-on contract to the same vendor
Settle outstanding claims and make final payment for accepted work
Re-open competition for the completed scope

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Financial closeout requires resolving open claims and disputes and issuing final payment for work performed and accepted, so the contract can be closed with no loose financial ends. Why the others are wrong: **A** destroying the file violates records-retention requirements and must not precede closeout; **B** awarding a follow-on contract is a separate acquisition and does not close this one; **D** re-opening competition for already-completed scope is illogical and unrelated to settling and closing.

questions.stem: A clause states that the contractor must pay a preset amount per day of late delivery, set as a reasonable forecast of the buyer's harm. This clause is BEST described as:

options.text: A liquidated damages clause
A penalty clause that courts routinely enforce
A warranty clause
An indemnification clause

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Liquidated damages set, in advance, a reasonable estimate of damages for a breach such as late delivery when actual damages would be hard to quantify; they are enforceable when not a penalty. Why the others are wrong: **B** a true penalty (punitive, not a reasonable estimate) is generally unenforceable, so labeling it an enforceable penalty is wrong; **C** a warranty addresses conformity/quality of goods, not delay damages; **D** indemnification shifts liability for third-party claims, not preset delay damages.

questions.stem: Arrange the steps of properly processing a contract change in the correct sequence, from first to last.

options.text: Identify the need for a change and document the proposed change
Analyze the change's impact on scope, schedule, cost, and risk
Negotiate and formally execute the modification with proper authority
Implement the change and update the contract records

questions.explanation: A change must first be identified and documented (A) so everyone agrees on what is proposed. Its impact is then analyzed across scope, schedule, cost, and risk (B) to inform negotiation. The parties negotiate and execute a formal modification signed by someone with authority (C); only after that is the change implemented and the contract records updated (D). Implementing before analysis or formal execution risks unauthorized commitments and disputes, so the order is identify, analyze, execute, then implement.

questions.stem: During contract closeout, what must be confirmed before the contract can be formally closed?

options.text: That all contractual obligations have been performed and accepted by both parties
That the next contract has already been awarded
That the contractor has hired new staff
That the buyer has issued a new solicitation

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Closeout begins with verifying that all obligations—deliverables, services, and administrative requirements—have been completed and accepted, which is the foundation for final payment and closure. Why the others are wrong: **B** awarding the next contract is unrelated to closing this one; **C** the contractor's staffing has no bearing on whether this contract's obligations are met; **D** issuing a new solicitation is a separate, future acquisition action.

questions.stem: Why are records retention requirements important during and after contract closeout?

options.text: They ensure documentation is preserved for the required period to support audits, claims, and disputes
They allow all contract files to be destroyed immediately at closeout
They are optional and have no compliance basis
They require records to be shared publicly without restriction

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Records retention preserves contract documentation for a defined period so the organization can support audits, respond to claims or disputes, and demonstrate compliance after closeout. Why the others are wrong: **B** immediate destruction at closeout would violate retention requirements and destroy evidence needed later; **C** retention is a real compliance obligation, not optional; **D** retained records often include proprietary or sensitive data and are not released publicly without restriction.

questions.stem: At the end of a contract, the team documents what went well and what should be improved so future contracts benefit. This practice is BEST described as:

options.text: Capturing lessons learned
Conducting market research
Performing a bid/no-bid analysis
Issuing a constructive change

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Lessons learned capture successes and problems and translate them into improvements for future acquisitions, a key closeout and continuous-improvement activity. Why the others are wrong: **B** market research is a pre-solicitation activity to inform a new buy; **C** a bid/no-bid analysis is the seller's pursuit decision before proposing; **D** a constructive change is a performance-phase event involving informal direction, not an end-of-contract review.

questions.stem: NCMA's Contract Management Standard organizes the discipline around two parties working through the life cycle. Which pairing of life-cycle phases is correct?

options.text: Design, build, and test
Marketing, sales, and collections
Pre-award, award, and post-award
Planning, hiring, and firing

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The Contract Management Standard frames the life cycle in three top-level phases—pre-award, award, and post-award—each containing buyer and seller activities. Why the others are wrong: **B** marketing, sales, and collections are business functions, not the contract life-cycle phases; **A** design, build, and test describe a product-development cycle, not contract management; **D** planning, hiring, and firing are general management actions unrelated to the standard's structure.

questions.stem: A junior contract manager is unsure whether a particular action is permissible. Their organization expects them to apply professional competencies as they grow. Which competency category covers a contract manager's grasp of business acumen, the discipline's leading practices, and applicable law?

options.text: Athletic ability
Office seniority
Personal hobbies
Knowledge competencies

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Knowledge competencies describe what a contract manager must understand—business, the contracting environment, leading practices, and applicable law—to perform effectively. Why the others are wrong: **A** athletic ability is irrelevant to professional contract-management competence; **C** personal hobbies are unrelated to the body of knowledge; **B** seniority is a tenure measure, not a defined competency a professional must develop.

questions.stem: A contract manager learns that their spouse owns a significant financial stake in a company about to bid on a procurement the manager is running. The MOST appropriate first action is to:

options.text: Say nothing because the stake belongs to the spouse, not the manager
Promptly disclose the relationship and recuse themselves from the procurement decision
Quietly steer the award to a different bidder to avoid the appearance of favoritism
Continue running the procurement but promise to be objective

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A financial interest held by a close family member creates a conflict of interest; the ethical response is prompt disclosure and recusal so an impartial party manages the procurement. Why the others are wrong: **A** a spouse's interest is imputed to the manager and cannot simply be ignored; **C** secretly steering the award to a different bidder is itself improper manipulation of the process; **D** a personal promise of objectivity does not cure a real conflict of interest.

questions.stem: A team is launching a high-stakes negotiation with an unfamiliar counterparty. Before engaging, the contract manager performs a situational assessment. The PRIMARY purpose of this assessment is to:

options.text: Decide which clauses to delete from the standard template at random
Understand the context, stakeholders, risks, and constraints so the approach can be tailored to the situation
Avoid all communication with the other party
Guarantee that no risks will materialize during performance

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A situational assessment examines the environment, stakeholders, risks, and constraints so the contract manager can adapt strategy, team dynamics, and communication to the specific situation. Why the others are wrong: **A** deleting clauses at random is arbitrary and unrelated to assessing a situation; **C** good situational management improves communication rather than eliminating it; **D** assessment informs risk handling but cannot guarantee no risk will occur.

questions.stem: Under a fixed-price incentive (firm target) contract, the parties set a target cost, target profit, ceiling price, and a share ratio. Once costs exceed the ceiling price, who absorbs the additional cost?

options.text: The buyer, because the ceiling caps the seller's exposure
It is shared by the original share ratio with no limit
The seller, because the ceiling price is the maximum the buyer will pay
A surety bond automatically covers the excess

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** In a fixed-price incentive (firm target) contract, costs are shared by the share ratio only up to the ceiling price; above the ceiling the seller bears 100% of further cost, since the ceiling is the maximum price the buyer will pay. Why the others are wrong: **A** the ceiling caps the buyer's payment, shifting overrun above it to the seller, not the buyer; **B** the share ratio stops applying once the ceiling (point of total assumption) is reached; **D** a surety bond guarantees performance or payment, it does not reimburse overruns.

questions.stem: Which two communication behaviors best support healthy team dynamics on a cross-functional contract team? (Select two.)

options.text: Actively listening to and clarifying others' concerns before responding
Sharing relevant information transparently with the appropriate stakeholders
Withholding bad news so the team stays optimistic
Making unilateral decisions without consulting affected functions

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Effective contract teams rely on active listening to surface concerns and on transparent, appropriate information sharing so everyone can act on accurate facts. Why the others are wrong: **C** withholding bad news deprives the team of information needed to manage risk and erodes trust; **D** unilateral decisions that ignore affected functions damage collaboration and lead to poor outcomes.

questions.stem: Before releasing a formal solicitation, a buyer wants to gauge industry interest and refine its draft requirement without committing to award. Which instrument is MOST appropriate?

options.text: A signed bilateral modification
A binding Invitation for Bids (IFB)
A Request for Information (RFI) or sources-sought notice
A notice of contract closeout

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** An RFI or sources-sought notice gathers market information and gauges interest to refine requirements and strategy, without obligating the buyer to award. Why the others are wrong: **B** an IFB is a binding solicitation that leads to award, not a low-commitment information-gathering step; **A** a bilateral modification changes an existing contract, unrelated to pre-solicitation research; **D** a closeout notice concerns ending a completed contract.

questions.stem: A buyer expects offerors to take exception to certain draft terms. To surface and resolve concerns and improve proposal quality before final offers are due, the buyer should:

options.text: Forbid any offeror contact until award to keep the process clean
Issue a draft solicitation and hold an industry/pre-proposal conference and a Q&A period
Change the evaluation criteria secretly after offers arrive
Award sole-source to avoid dealing with multiple offerors

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Releasing a draft solicitation and conducting a pre-proposal conference with a formal Q&A lets offerors raise concerns and ambiguities early, improving the final solicitation and the quality of offers. Why the others are wrong: **A** prohibiting all contact prevents clarification and worsens proposal quality; **C** secretly changing criteria after receipt is an integrity violation; **D** defaulting to sole-source to avoid engagement abandons competition without justification.

questions.stem: A buyer drafting a services solicitation wants offerors to propose how to achieve outcomes rather than dictating exact methods. Which type of work description BEST fits this goal?

options.text: A design (detailed) specification that prescribes exact steps and materials
A performance work statement that states required outcomes and measurable standards
A blank purchase order with no description
A copy of the buyer's internal budget

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A performance work statement (PWS) defines the required results and measurable performance standards, giving offerors latitude to propose the best method to achieve them. Why the others are wrong: **A** a design specification dictates exact methods/materials, the opposite of outcome-based; **C** a blank purchase order provides no basis to propose or evaluate; **D** an internal budget is not a work description and is not disclosed to offerors.

questions.stem: A solicitation will award to the offer that provides the best combination of non-price factors and price, allowing the buyer to pay a premium for superior technical merit. This award basis is known as:

options.text: Lowest-price technically acceptable (LPTA)
Best-value tradeoff
Reverse auction by price only
Random selection

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A best-value tradeoff award lets the buyer weigh non-price factors against price and select a higher-priced offer when its superior merit justifies the premium. Why the others are wrong: **A** LPTA awards to the lowest price that meets a pass/fail standard, with no premium for extra merit; **C** a price-only reverse auction ignores non-price factors entirely; **D** random selection is not a valid evaluation basis.

questions.stem: A buyer must purchase an indefinite quantity of repair parts over a year, with exact amounts unknown but a guaranteed minimum to be ordered. Which contract vehicle BEST fits?

options.text: A firm-fixed-price contract for a single fixed quantity
A cost-plus-fixed-fee research contract
A one-time purchase order for the full year of parts
An indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ) contract with stated minimum and maximum

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** An IDIQ contract is designed for an indefinite quantity of supplies or services within a fixed period, with a guaranteed minimum and a ceiling maximum, filled through individual orders. Why the others are wrong: **A** a single fixed-quantity FFP cannot accommodate unknown, recurring quantities; **C** a one-time purchase order for an unknown full-year quantity is impractical and risky; **B** a CPFF research contract addresses uncertain R&D scope, not recurring known parts.

questions.stem: When selecting a contract type for a new acquisition, which two factors most strongly drive the choice between a fixed-price and a cost-reimbursement arrangement? (Select two.)

options.text: The degree of uncertainty in the requirement and the ability to estimate cost
How the cost and performance risk should be allocated between buyer and seller
The favorite color of the contracting officer
Whether the contract number is even or odd

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Contract-type selection turns on how well the requirement can be defined and costed and on the desired allocation of cost/performance risk—well-defined work favors fixed price (seller risk), while high uncertainty favors cost reimbursement (buyer risk). Why the others are wrong: **C** a personal color preference is irrelevant to risk and pricing; **D** the parity of a contract number has no bearing on contract-type selection.

questions.stem: A seller's capture team builds a strategy to position the company favorably with the buyer well before the RFP is released. This pre-RFP positioning work is BEST described as:

options.text: Cost analysis
Contract closeout
Capture planning
Quality surveillance

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Capture planning is the seller's pre-RFP effort to understand the customer, shape the opportunity, and position the company to win before the solicitation is released. Why the others are wrong: **B** closeout occurs at the end of a contract, not during opportunity pursuit; **A** cost analysis is the buyer's evaluation of an offeror's cost elements; **D** quality surveillance happens during performance, not pre-RFP sales planning.

questions.stem: During proposal pricing, a seller must apply indirect cost rates to its direct base. An indirect cost is BEST defined as a cost that:

options.text: Can be identified specifically with a single final cost objective
Is incurred for common or joint objectives and cannot be traced to one contract, so it is allocated across many
Is always disallowed and may never be billed
Equals the seller's profit on the contract

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Indirect costs (e.g., overhead, G&A) benefit common or joint objectives and cannot be traced to a single contract, so they are pooled and allocated across cost objectives via rates. Why the others are wrong: **A** a cost traceable to one final cost objective is a direct cost, not indirect; **C** indirect costs are routinely allowable and billable when allocable and reasonable; **D** profit/fee is a separate element, not the definition of indirect cost.

questions.stem: A seller assembles a proposal volume and notices that price is the only completed section while the technical and management volumes are missing. To submit a fully responsive offer, the seller must ensure the proposal:

options.text: Substitutes the seller's marketing brochure for the required volumes
Contains only the lowest possible price and nothing else
Omits the management approach because evaluators rarely read it
Addresses every section and requirement the solicitation instructs offerors to provide

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A responsive offer must address every section and requirement the solicitation directs offerors to submit; missing required volumes can render the proposal unacceptable. Why the others are wrong: **B** price alone ignores mandatory technical and management content; **C** omitting a required management volume is non-compliant regardless of assumptions about evaluators; **A** a generic brochure does not satisfy the specific required volumes.

questions.stem: A seller wins a fixed-price contract by deliberately bidding below its expected cost, planning to recover the loss through change orders during performance. This pricing approach is BEST described as:

options.text: A buy-in, which carries the risk that anticipated recoveries may not materialize
A best-value tradeoff favored by buyers
A liquidated damages strategy
A novation of the contract

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A buy-in is submitting a price below anticipated cost intending to recoup through later changes or follow-ons; it is risky because the expected recoveries may never occur, leaving the seller to absorb the loss. Why the others are wrong: **B** a best-value tradeoff is a buyer's award method, not a seller's underbidding tactic; **C** liquidated damages are preset breach damages, unrelated to underpricing; **D** a novation substitutes a contract party, not a pricing strategy.

questions.stem: A seller wants an independent internal team to challenge a draft proposal as if they were the source-selection evaluators, scoring its strengths and weaknesses before submission. This practice is commonly called a:

options.text: Sole-source justification
Termination for convenience
Constructive change
Color-team (e.g., red team) review

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Color-team reviews (such as a red team) use an independent group to evaluate a draft proposal against the solicitation as the customer would, exposing weaknesses while there is still time to fix them. Why the others are wrong: **B** termination for convenience ends a contract after award; **C** a constructive change is a performance-phase event; **A** a sole-source justification supports awarding without competition, not reviewing a proposal.

questions.stem: Which two are legitimate ways for a seller to manage performance risk it identifies during proposal preparation? (Select two.)

options.text: Propose a risk mitigation plan and include realistic contingency in cost or schedule
Negotiate to shift appropriate risk via the contract type or specific terms
Conceal the risk and hope it does not occur
Inflate the fee arbitrarily with no link to the identified risk

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Sellers manage identified risk by planning credible mitigations with appropriate contingency and by negotiating an allocation of risk through the contract type and specific terms. Why the others are wrong: **C** concealing risk leads to underpricing and performance failure; **D** arbitrarily inflating fee without tying it to a real risk is not sound risk management and weakens competitiveness.

questions.stem: Under a competitive best-value procurement, the buyer establishes a competitive range and then conducts discussions. The purpose of a competitive range is to:

options.text: Identify the offers with a reasonable chance of award so discussions focus on those offerors
Eliminate every offeror so the buyer can cancel the procurement
Disclose each offeror's price to all competitors
Replace the need to evaluate proposals

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The competitive range comprises the most highly rated offers—those with a reasonable chance of award—so the buyer can hold meaningful discussions with viable offerors rather than all of them. Why the others are wrong: **B** the range narrows competition to viable offerors, not to cancel the buy; **C** disclosing competitors' prices would breach procurement integrity; **D** establishing a range follows evaluation; it does not replace it.

questions.stem: After discussions in a negotiated procurement, the buyer asks offerors in the competitive range to submit their best and final pricing and revisions. This request is commonly called the:

options.text: Final proposal revision (best and final offer)
Cure notice
Show-cause notice
Notice to proceed

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** After discussions, the buyer requests final proposal revisions—historically the best and final offer (BAFO)—giving offerors a single opportunity to submit their best terms before the award decision. Why the others are wrong: **B** a cure notice addresses a contractor's failure to perform after award; **C** a show-cause notice precedes a potential default termination; **D** a notice to proceed authorizes performance to begin, not a final pricing submission.

questions.stem: Two negotiators each have a strong alternative if no deal is reached. In negotiation theory, the strength of a party's best alternative to a negotiated agreement (BATNA) primarily affects:

options.text: The party's bargaining power and willingness to walk away
The color of the contract cover page
The requirement to use sealed bidding
The contractor's records-retention period

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A strong BATNA increases a party's bargaining power because it can credibly walk away if the deal is worse than its alternative, anchoring its reservation point. Why the others are wrong: **B** document formatting has nothing to do with negotiating leverage; **C** sealed bidding is a solicitation method, unrelated to BATNA; **D** records retention is a closeout/administration matter, not a negotiation lever.

questions.stem: A buyer suspects an offeror's proposed price is unrealistically low for the required effort, raising doubt about the offeror's understanding of the work. This concern is BEST analyzed through:

options.text: A novation review
A liquidated damages calculation
A price-realism analysis
A records-retention audit

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Price-realism analysis assesses whether proposed prices are realistic for the work, reflecting a clear understanding of requirements and the risk of performance problems from an unrealistically low price. Why the others are wrong: **B** liquidated damages address late or deficient performance after award, not bid realism; **A** a novation concerns substituting a contracting party; **D** a records-retention audit is a closeout/compliance check, not price evaluation.

questions.stem: A contract incorporates a separate technical exhibit "by reference." Under contract interpretation, a document incorporated by reference is generally:

options.text: Treated as part of the contract, as if its terms were written into the agreement
Legally irrelevant because it is not physically attached
Binding only on the buyer, never the seller
Automatically superior to every other contract clause

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A document properly incorporated by reference becomes part of the contract and binds the parties as though its terms were set out in full. Why the others are wrong: **B** valid incorporation by reference is effective even though the document is not physically attached; **C** an incorporated document binds both parties, not just the buyer; **D** incorporation does not make a document automatically superior—order-of-precedence clauses govern conflicts.

questions.stem: A contract's clauses conflict: the schedule says one thing and an attached specification says another. To resolve which provision controls, the contract manager should consult the:

options.text: Warranty clause
Termination for convenience clause
Limitation-of-cost clause
Order-of-precedence clause

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** An order-of-precedence clause establishes the hierarchy among conflicting contract parts, so the manager applies the ranking to determine which provision controls. Why the others are wrong: **B** a termination-for-convenience clause governs ending the contract, not internal conflicts; **C** a limitation-of-cost clause concerns funding on cost-type contracts; **A** a warranty clause addresses conformity of goods, not document precedence.

questions.stem: A party seeks to be excused from timely performance because of an extraordinary event beyond its control, such as a natural disaster. The clause that typically excuses such non-performance is a:

options.text: Force majeure / excusable delay clause
Assignment clause
Confidentiality clause
Audit clause

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A force majeure or excusable-delay clause relieves a party from liability for delay or non-performance caused by extraordinary events beyond its reasonable control, such as natural disasters. Why the others are wrong: **B** an assignment clause governs transferring contract rights or obligations; **C** a confidentiality clause protects sensitive information; **D** an audit clause grants rights to examine records, none of which excuse delay.

questions.stem: Which two practices help ensure a documented, defensible source-selection decision? (Select two.)

options.text: Recording how each offer was scored against the stated evaluation factors
Preparing a written award decision that traces the rationale to the criteria
Selecting the offeror before evaluating any proposals
Applying undisclosed criteria that were never in the solicitation

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A defensible selection records scoring against the stated factors and produces a written decision whose rationale traces directly to those criteria. Why the others are wrong: **C** choosing the offeror before evaluation is arbitrary and indefensible; **D** applying undisclosed criteria violates fairness and exposes the award to protest.

questions.stem: Immediately after award, the buyer and contractor hold a meeting to align on roles, communication channels, key milestones, and administrative procedures. This meeting is BEST described as a:

options.text: Source-selection board
Bid/no-bid review
Post-award (kickoff) conference
Closeout audit

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A post-award or kickoff conference aligns the parties on roles, communication, milestones, reporting, and administrative procedures at the start of performance. Why the others are wrong: **B** a bid/no-bid review is the seller's pre-proposal decision; **A** a source-selection board operates pre-award to evaluate offers; **D** a closeout audit occurs at the end of the contract, not its start.

questions.stem: On a federal-style contract, only one official holds the authority to bind the government by entering into, modifying, or terminating the contract. That individual is the:

options.text: Contracting officer (with actual authority within delegated limits)
Any project engineer on the team
The contractor's program manager
Any end user who receives the deliverable

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Only the contracting officer holds actual authority, within delegated limits, to enter into, modify, or terminate the contract and bind the buyer. Why the others are wrong: **B** a project engineer lacks contracting authority and cannot bind the buyer; **C** the contractor's program manager represents the seller, not the buyer's binding authority; **D** an end user receiving deliverables has no authority to commit the organization contractually.

questions.stem: A contractor encountered a buyer-caused delay that increased its costs and now seeks more money under the contract's changes clause. The formal price/schedule adjustment that compensates the contractor for such a change is called a(n):

options.text: Cure notice
Liquidated damage
Novation
Equitable adjustment

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** An equitable adjustment modifies the contract price and/or schedule to fairly compensate the contractor for the cost and time impact of a change, including certain buyer-caused delays. Why the others are wrong: **B** liquidated damages are amounts the contractor pays the buyer for late performance, the opposite direction; **C** a novation substitutes a contracting party; **A** a cure notice demands correction of a performance failure, not compensation for a change.

questions.stem: A buyer issues a one-sided contract modification, signed only by the contracting officer, directing a change within the scope of the contract's changes clause. This is an example of a(n):

options.text: Unilateral modification
Bilateral supplemental agreement
Teaming agreement
Mutual rescission

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A unilateral modification is signed only by the buyer and is used for actions the contract already authorizes, such as a change ordered within the scope of the changes clause or an administrative change. Why the others are wrong: **B** a bilateral supplemental agreement requires both parties' signatures; **C** a teaming agreement is a pre-award arrangement between firms; **D** a mutual rescission cancels the contract by agreement, not a directed in-scope change.

questions.stem: A prime contractor flows a key clause down to its subcontractor and remains answerable to the buyer for the subcontractor's work. Regarding that subcontractor, the prime contractor's responsibility to the buyer is BEST described as:

options.text: Eliminated, because the subcontractor now deals directly with the buyer
Retained, because privity is between the buyer and the prime, who remains responsible for total performance
Limited to introducing the subcontractor to the buyer
Transferred entirely to the buyer's contracting officer

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Contractual privity runs between the buyer and the prime; the prime remains responsible to the buyer for total performance, including work it subcontracts, which is why critical clauses are flowed down. Why the others are wrong: **A** subcontracting does not create privity between the buyer and subcontractor or relieve the prime; **C** the prime's duty far exceeds making an introduction; **D** responsibility is not transferred to the buyer's contracting officer.

questions.stem: A buyer wants to track a services contractor's actual results against measurable standards using a structured surveillance approach throughout performance. The document that defines what will be monitored and how is the:

options.text: Quality assurance surveillance plan (QASP)
Bid/no-bid memo
Source-selection plan
Final invoice

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A QASP defines the performance standards, surveillance methods, and acceptable quality levels the buyer uses to monitor a services contractor during performance. Why the others are wrong: **B** a bid/no-bid memo is the seller's pursuit decision before proposing; **C** a source-selection plan governs evaluating offers pre-award; **D** a final invoice is a closeout payment document, not a surveillance tool.

questions.stem: A contractor and buyer cannot resolve a dispute over entitlement to additional costs. On a federal-style contract, the contractor formally submits a written demand seeking a contracting officer's final decision. This submission is a:

options.text: Quotation
Bid
Claim
Solicitation amendment

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A claim is a written demand seeking, as a matter of right, payment, adjustment, or interpretation of terms, on which the contracting officer renders a final decision that can then be appealed. Why the others are wrong: **B** a bid is an offer in sealed bidding, not a dispute demand; **A** a quotation is an informational price response, not a binding claim; **D** a solicitation amendment changes a solicitation before award, unrelated to a performance dispute.

questions.stem: As part of closing out a completed contract, the buyer records a formal evaluation of how well the contractor performed on cost, schedule, and quality, to inform future source selections. The PRIMARY purpose of this past-performance evaluation is to:

options.text: Create a documented performance record that can be considered in evaluating the contractor on future competitions
Reopen the completed contract for renegotiation of price
Replace the need to verify that deliverables were accepted
Serve as the contractor's final invoice

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A closeout past-performance evaluation documents how well the contractor met cost, schedule, and quality requirements, creating a record that buyers may consider as past performance in future source selections. Why the others are wrong: **B** the evaluation does not reopen or renegotiate the completed contract; **C** confirming acceptance of deliverables is a separate closeout step that the evaluation does not replace; **D** an invoice is a payment document, not a performance assessment.

questions.stem: A latent defect is discovered in delivered equipment after the buyer had already accepted it. Under a standard warranty clause, the buyer's typical remedy is to:

options.text: Pay the contractor a bonus for the defective item
Forfeit all remedies because acceptance always ends every right
Automatically terminate the contractor for convenience
Require the contractor to repair or replace the nonconforming item within the warranty terms

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A warranty extends the buyer's rights beyond acceptance, allowing it to require repair or replacement of items that fail to conform within the warranty period and terms. Why the others are wrong: **B** acceptance generally does not bar remedies for latent defects or breach of warranty; **C** termination for convenience is a buyer's discretionary action, not the warranty remedy; **A** paying a bonus for a defective item is illogical and contrary to remedy principles.

questions.stem: Which two are appropriate contract administration responses when a contractor begins to fall behind schedule? (Select two.)

options.text: Document the slippage and request a corrective action plan from the contractor
Increase performance monitoring and assess the impact on milestones and remedies
Ignore the delay until the final delivery date passes
Approve full payment for incomplete work to motivate the contractor

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** When performance slips, the administrator documents it, requests a corrective action plan, and increases monitoring while evaluating the impact on milestones and available remedies. Why the others are wrong: **C** ignoring the delay forfeits the chance to recover and protect the buyer's interests; **D** paying in full for incomplete work violates payment-for-performance principles and removes leverage.

questions.stem: A buyer is dissatisfied with a contractor's performance and is moving toward a possible default termination on a federal-style contract. Arrange the typical steps in the correct sequence, from first to last.

options.text: Identify and document the contractor's failure to meet a contractual requirement
Issue a cure notice giving the contractor an opportunity to fix the deficiency
If uncured, issue a show-cause notice requesting reasons the contract should not be terminated
Make the termination-for-default decision and issue the termination notice

questions.explanation: The process begins by identifying and documenting the specific failure (A), establishing the factual basis. The buyer then issues a cure notice (B) giving the contractor a chance to fix the deficiency within a set period. If the deficiency is not cured, a show-cause notice (C) asks the contractor to explain why the contract should not be terminated, building the record. Only after these steps does the buyer make the termination-for-default decision and issue the notice (D). Note that under FAR 49.402-3 a cure notice is not required before terminating for a contractor's failure to deliver supplies or perform services on time; it is required only when terminating for failure to make progress or to perform some other provision of the contract. Where a cure notice does apply, skipping the cure and show-cause steps risks an improper, reversible default, so the order is identify, cure, show-cause, then terminate.

questions.stem: Near the end of performance, the contract administrator works through a structured list confirming that all deliverables are accepted, property is dispositioned, and final invoices are received. This tool is BEST described as a:

options.text: Source-selection scorecard
Bid/no-bid matrix
Closeout checklist
Market research report

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A closeout checklist guides the administrator through the required completion actions—verifying accepted deliverables, property disposition, final invoices, and documentation—so nothing is missed before closing. Why the others are wrong: **B** a bid/no-bid matrix supports a seller's pursuit decision; **A** a source-selection scorecard is used pre-award to evaluate offers; **D** a market research report informs a new acquisition, not closeout.

questions.stem: At the close of a cost-reimbursement contract, the parties must reconcile billed costs to the contractor's audited actual indirect rates before final payment. This reconciliation step is part of:

options.text: Final indirect cost rate settlement and financial closeout
Issuing a new solicitation
Conducting market research
Preparing a bid/no-bid decision

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** On cost-reimbursement contracts, financial closeout includes settling final indirect cost rates so that amounts billed at provisional rates are reconciled to audited actual rates before final payment. Why the others are wrong: **B** issuing a new solicitation is a separate, future acquisition; **C** market research informs a new buy, not rate settlement; **D** a bid/no-bid decision is the seller's pre-proposal step, unrelated to closing out costs.

questions.stem: After a contract closes, a contract manager pursues professional development and reflects on captured lessons to strengthen future performance. Within the body of knowledge, this ongoing self-improvement is BEST described as:

options.text: Continuous learning and competence development
A constructive change
An equitable adjustment
A unilateral modification

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Continuous learning and competence development is the professional's commitment to ongoing growth—applying lessons learned and building skills to improve future contract outcomes. Why the others are wrong: **B** a constructive change is an informal direction event during performance; **C** an equitable adjustment is a price/schedule remedy for a change; **D** a unilateral modification is a buyer-signed contract change, none of which describe personal development.

questions.stem: A contract manager describes their job as guiding an agreement so that, at the end, the organization actually received what it bargained for and the relationship can continue. Within NCMA's framework, this outcome-focused orientation is BEST captured by the guiding principle that contract management exists to:

options.text: Generate the maximum number of contract documents per quarter
Deliver value to the organization by achieving the intended business outcomes of the agreement
Ensure the legal department wins every dispute
Keep the supplier permanently dependent on the buyer

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The discipline's guiding purpose is to deliver value by helping the organization achieve the business outcomes the contract was meant to produce, not merely to process paperwork. Why the others are wrong: **A** counting documents measures activity, not value; **C** winning disputes is sometimes necessary but is not the purpose of contract management; **D** fostering supplier dependence is not a value-delivery goal.

questions.stem: A contract manager is asked to certify on an invoice that work was completed when they personally have no knowledge that it was. Their supervisor pressures them to sign "to keep things moving." The MOST consistent action with professional standards of conduct is to:

options.text: Sign the certification to satisfy the supervisor and avoid conflict
Refuse to certify what they cannot verify and escalate the pressure appropriately
Sign but add a note that they were told to do so
